n: Joseph’s story resumes in Egypt. He is bought by Potiphar, a high-ranking Egyptian official—a slave in a foreign land, far from his father.
The key line of this chapter: “the LORD was with Joseph.” Even as a slave, Joseph succeeded because God was with him.
Potiphar, a pagan, could see that Joseph’s success came from his God. Faithful lives often testify of God without words.
Potiphar trusted Joseph so fully that he made him manager of his entire household and estate.
God blessed Potiphar’s whole household because of Joseph—fulfilling the covenant promise that Abraham’s family would bless others.
Potiphar worried about nothing except what he ate. The note that Joseph was handsome sets up the temptation that follows.

f.g: knew of nothing, didn’t concern himself with anything

n: Potiphar’s wife tried to seduce Joseph, bluntly and repeatedly. Joseph faced a test of character as a young man alone in a foreign land.
Joseph refused, first pointing to his loyalty to his master, who had trusted him with everything.

f.g: does not know (does not concern himself with)

n: Joseph’s deepest reason: such an act would be sin against God. He saw that morality is ultimately about our relationship with God.

f.w: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?

n: She kept pressing him day after day, and Joseph not only refused but avoided being with her at all—a wise way to resist ongoing temptation.

f.g: did not listen or give in

n: One day Joseph came in to work and found no other servants in the house—the moment she had waited for.
She grabbed his garment, and Joseph fled, leaving it in her hand. Sometimes the right response to temptation is simply to run.

f.g: For the second time Joseph loses a garment, and again it is used to tell a lie.

n: Holding his garment and rejected, she quickly turned it into evidence against him.
She called the servants and accused Joseph, stirring up resentment by calling him “an Hebrew,” an outsider, and blaming her husband for bringing him.

f.g: to insult or take liberties with us
A term often used by foreigners for Abraham’s descendants.

n: She twisted the facts: the garment Joseph left as he fled became “proof” he had attacked her.
She kept the garment beside her as evidence until Potiphar came home.
She repeated the false charge to her husband, subtly blaming him for bringing “the Hebrew servant” into the house.
Her story stays consistent, and the garment seems to confirm it. Joseph is given no chance to defend himself.
Potiphar became furious. Some readers note he did not execute Joseph, which might mean he had doubts about his wife’s story.
Joseph was put in the royal prison where the king’s prisoners were held. Doing right had cost him dearly—for now.
Even in prison the refrain returns: the Lord was with Joseph. God’s presence is not limited to good circumstances.
The warden put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners. As in Potiphar’s house, Joseph rose through faithful service.
The warden stopped worrying about anything Joseph handled, because the Lord made Joseph succeed. The pattern of the chapter is complete: in every setting God blesses the faithful.

f.g: did not need to supervise anything
